hints: Focus on the shape of the Boltzmann curve, a higher temperature flattens the peak and pushes more molecules out to high energy.
Compare P and Q, Q is lower and broader with a longer tail at high energy, so Q must be the hotter sample.
Remember what a catalyst does, it provides a route of lower activation energy, so look for the line at lower molecular energy.
walkthrough:
**Spot the hotter curve**

Think of heating as spreading energy out. The peak gets lower and the curve gets broader, with more molecules at high energy.

Rule: higher $T$ = lower peak maximum, shifted right, larger area beyond $E_a$.

**Compare P and Q**

Curve P is tall and narrow with most molecules at low to medium energy. Curve Q is shorter, flatter and stretches further to the right.

That means Q has the greater proportion of molecules with high energy, so Q is the higher temperature.

**Spot the catalysed activation energy**

A catalyst speeds up reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. It does not change the Boltzmann curve itself.

$$E_{a}(catalysed) < E_{a}(uncatalysed)$$

**Pick X or Y**

Line X is at lower molecular energy than line Y. So X is the lowered, catalysed $E_a$ and Y is the uncatalysed $E_a$.

Combine them: higher temperature is Q plus catalyst present is X.

options.A: Incorrect. P is the lower temperature curve because it is taller, narrower and has fewer molecules at high energy. X is correct for the catalyst, but the temperature part is wrong.
options.B: Incorrect on both parts. P is the colder curve, not the hotter one, and Y is the higher activation energy, which is the uncatalysed route.
options.C: Correct. Q is broader, lower-peaked and has more molecules beyond $E_a$, so it is the higher temperature. X is at lower energy than Y, so it is the lowered activation energy provided by the catalyst.
options.D: Half right, half wrong. Q is indeed the higher temperature, but Y is the higher activation energy for the reaction without a catalyst. A catalyst would lower $E_a$ to X.
